newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to trim wheat export estimate, raise barley.
newsitem.headline: France to trim wheat export estimate, raise barley.

text.p: French wheat exports look set to end the season slightly lower than previously expected after problems in executing sales to Iraq -- but will still be 70 percent up on last year, industry sources said on Friday.
France's ONIC cereals office last month projected commercial soft wheat sales to the world market of 6.45 million tonnes in the 1996/97 season ending on June 30.

That figure seems likely to be closer to 6.3 million tonnes when ONIC puts out its next supply/demand report on June 11, but the fall should be partly offset by higher sales to the rest of the European Union, the sources said.

France is now thought to have exported just over 9.4 million tonnes of wheat within the EU this season compared with 9.36 million tonnes projected by ONIC last month and 8.613 million tonnes in 1995/96.
Exports to non-EU countries in 1995/96 were an unusually low 3.75 million tonnes because of tight supplies.

The sources said roughly 350,000 tonnes of wheat had been shipped from France to Iraq under the U.N. oil-for-food deal, but this was somewhat lower than expected after delays in obtaining U.N. approval for contracts.
The changes are expected to leave French carryover stocks at above 2.2 million tonnes, compared with 2.12 million tonnes forecast last month and 2.204 million last season.

French 1996/97 barley exports are now seen at 1.6 million tonnes rather than the 1.5 million projected last month, the sources said. But this is almost entirely offset by lower estimates for exports to the EU, last estimated at 2.46 million.
A new barley carryover of some 870,000 tonnes is higher than the 600,000 tonnes usually considered the operational norm for the French domestic market between seasons, the sources said.

So the fact that only 16,000 tonnes of barley was offered into intervention in France this year indicates that around 270,000 tonnes of "precautionary stock" is being held back, possibly because of anxieties over malting quality, they said.
